title: Ed Yardeni spots a major shakeup in the S&P 500
detail:
Ed Yardeni spots a major shakeup in the S&P 500
Moz Farooque
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 11:18 AM MST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
TSLA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

You don't need to own shares of Nvidia (NVDA) or Tesla (TSLA) individually to have a sizable bet on Big Tech.

Anyone who owns an S&P 500 index fund already owns both, along with other stocks that comprise the Magnificent Seven. Collectively, those seven companies account for nearly 35% of the benchmark. 

Truth be told, for the better part of the past three years, that concentration was a good thing. Big Tech powered the market higher, driving record gains in retirement and brokerage accounts.

For perspective, Fidelity Investments reported that average 401(k) balances reached a record $155,800 in Q2 2026, up 13% year over year, backed by market gains and continued savings.

Also read: 40-year market veteran shares S&P 500 outlook for 2027

But something has changed in 2026.

Wall Street veteran Ed Yardeni, who has spent years favoring major technology stocks, says the S&P 500's other 493 companies are now outperforming the celebrated seven.

And he thinks the shift has a lot to do with who's paying for the AI boom, and who's positioned to profit from it.

Ed Yardeni says S&P 493 stocks are now outperforming the Magnificent Seven.
ANGELA WEISS / Getty Images
The Magnificent Seven are no longer running away from the S&P 493 

For years, especially since the AI boom took off following the release of OpenAI's ChatGPT, betting on America's biggest tech companies has been one of the easiest ways to outperform the broader stock market.

The Magnificent Seven, which includes Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Nvidia (NVDA), Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL), Meta Platforms (META), and Tesla (TSLA), were almost unstoppable.

In 2023, the group surged 76%, compared with just 11% for the other 493 companies in the S&P 500, according to J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

The dominance persisted in 2024, when the seven gained 48% versus 14% for the rest. In 2025, they won again, returning 23% compared with 13%.

That's a tremendous run, particularly given how much these stocks influence the retirement accounts and index funds owned by millions of Americans.

But 2026 is telling a different story.

In his October 19 market commentary, veteran Wall Street strategist Ed Yardeni reported that his "Impressive 493" had gained 14.1% year-to-date, outperforming the Magnificent Seven's 10.2%, based on his ETF comparison.

Yardeni foresees a shakeup coming.

In December 2025, after roughly 15 years of favoring major technology stocks, he recommended underweighting the Magnificent Seven, anticipating stronger competition and better opportunities elsewhere in the market, as reported by Reuters.

Interestingly, the shift isn't happening because Big Tech's profits have fallen off a cliff.

Since Elon Musk's Tesla Inc (NASDAQ:TSLA) and SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) share business relationships, investors wonder when a potential merger between the two companies will unfold.

With both companies reporting financial results this week, Benzinga polled its "PreMarket Playbook" audience to gauge how retail investors feel about the potential timing of a deal. "Do you think $SPCX and $TSLA will merge?" Benzinga asked the show's viewers on Friday, Oct. 16. These are the results:

Yes – but not until 2027 or later: 48%

No – stays separate: 25%

Yes – by TSLA annual meeting: 22%

Roadster flies first: 5%

To put the results into perspective, 70% of viewers think the merger will happen, either by Dec. 3 or sometime into the future.

Twenty-five percent of voters said the companies will remain separate.

"PreMarket Playbook" airs Monday through Friday at 8 a.m. ET on Benzinga's YouTube channel. The latest poll included responses from 100 viewers.

These odds from Benzinga viewers differ from prediction market Kalshi.

On Kalshi, the odds of the two companies merging before Jan. 1 2027 stand at only 15%. With the annual meeting date coming before then, 25% of Benzinga viewers predict a merger before then.

The odds of a merger being completed by April 1, 2027 stand at 49% on Kalshi. The Benzinga poll shows that nearly a majority (48%) predict a merger in 2027 or later. While it's hard to pinpoint an exact month next year when viewers expect the merger to happen, the poll is likely more optimistic about it happening than the prediction odds.

Read Also:Tesla Stock: 73% Of Benzinga Viewers Have Owned It. Here's How Many Still Do.

What Experts Say

Future Fund Managing Partner Gary Black said a merger between SpaceX and Tesla is "inevitable" because Musk has significant control over the votes in both companies.

Black cautions that a merger may not be as big a win as some investors expect because of "massive dilution" and the stock-for-stock deal. Black predicts SpaceX bidding $420 per share for Tesla.

RBC Capital analyst Tom Narayan recently predicted that SpaceX will acquire Tesla for $480 per share, valuing the combined companies at $3.74 trillion.

The analyst predicts that Tesla shareholders would own around 48% of the combined business.

Gerber Kawasaki CEO Ross Gerber said a potential merger is more likely after Tesla demonstrated the Roadster's flight capabilities. The move "has become obvious," Gerber said.

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) reports third-quarter earnings after the bell Tuesday, with its call at 4:30 p.m. ET.

Analysts expect earnings of 14 cents a share on $12.74 billion in revenue, up 63% from last quarter. SpaceX shares plunged nearly 14% after its previous earnings beat.

On Kalshi, traders are betting on what CEO Elon Musk and his team will say. AI terms crowd the top of the board, while a possible Tesla merger adds intrigue.

What Kalshi Predicts SpaceX Will Say

"Starlink" leads at 99%, with "Starship" at 98%. SpaceX ended June with 12 million Starlink subscribers; analysts project another 1.5 million to 1.8 million additions this quarter.

"Grok" trades at 97%, "Cursor" at 96% and "Data Center" at 93%. SpaceX rents out computing power from its Colossus data centers, with new cloud deals adding $1.6 billion in second-quarter revenue, nearly two-thirds of its AI division's total.

The company signed $14.1 billion in cloud-services contracts. CFO Bret Johnsen said new compute investments pay back in under a year, although the AI division posted a $1.26 billion operating loss. SpaceX bought Cursor for $60 billion in August.

"Moon" sits at 84%. NASA targets a crewed lunar landing in 2028, giving SpaceX a nearer-term deadline than Musk's Mars ambitions.

"Starmind" trades at 81%, "Colossus" at 78% and "Nvidia" at 74%. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is helping design orbital AI computers based on its Vera Rubin technology, while SpaceX's terrestrial AI computing capacity reached 1.4 gigawatts in June.

What Kalshi Predicts SpaceX Will Skip

"Mars" trades at 38% and "Artemis," NASA's lunar program, at 36%. Traders expect the Moon to come up, but not necessarily by program name, and they're skeptical Musk pivots to Mars.

"Tesla" trades at 59%, down 25 points, while "Combine / Combining" sits at just 24%.

RBC Capital Markets modeled a hypothetical takeover of Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) at $480 a share, creating a $3.74 trillion company. RBC says it knows of no actual deal. Tesla reports Wednesday.

"Starshield" sits at just 15%, days after restrictions disrupted Ukrainian drone operations. Reuters reported the order came from inside the White House, while Musk said the U.S. government controls the military satellite system. Four U.S. senators demanded answers from SpaceX on Monday.

"T-Mobile" sits at just 8%. The carrier currently partners with SpaceX to provide satellite phone coverage, but Musk's company has agreed to buy $8 billion in wireless spectrum previously owned by T-Mobile. The deal could help SpaceX build its own mobile network and compete directly with its partner.
